slides.title: 4.1.1 Creating and Connecting Nodes
keyPoints: Creating a new node before changing the existing list keeps allocation failure from disturbing accepted state.
To insert at the front, the new node takes ownership of the old head and the head then takes ownership of the new.
There is no shared ownership cycle because every owning edge points forward.
Separate a node’s payload from its structural role.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 4, treat 4.1.1 Creating and Connecting Nodes as an algorithmic claim. Creating a new node before changing the existing list keeps allocation failure from disturbing accepted state. To insert at the front, the new node takes ownership of the old head and the head then takes ownership of the new node. There is no shared ownership cycle because every owning edge points forward. A raw pointer used during traversal borrows a node while the list remains valid. It must not delete the node or survive an erasure that removes it. The ownership graph and traversal graph happen to share a direction, but their roles remain conceptually distinct. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: 4.2 Implementing Doubly Linked Lists

The extra links enable reverse traversal but also add invariants: the first node has no predecessor, each next.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 4, treat 4.2 Implementing Doubly Linked Lists as an algorithmic claim. A doubly linked list adds backward navigation. The extra links enable reverse traversal but also add invariants: the first node has no predecessor, each next node points back to its predecessor, and the tail identifies the last node or is null for an empty list. Make one direction owning and the reverse direction observing. Making both directions unique owners is impossible, while making both shared owners can create retention cycles. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. slides.title: 4.2.1 Maintaining Previous and Next Links
keyPoints: Each node’s next pointer owns its successor, while previous and the list’s tail are raw observers.
Appending prepares a new node, connects it through the old tail or head, and updates the tail observer only after.
Erasure must repair both directions.
A doubly linked list adds a reverse navigation path, not necessarily a second ownership path.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 4, treat 4.2.1 Maintaining Previous and Next Links as an algorithmic claim. Each node’s next pointer owns its successor, while previous and the list’s tail are raw observers. Appending prepares a new node, connects it through the old tail or head, and updates the tail observer only after ownership is established. Erasure must repair both directions. The successor’s previous pointer becomes the removed node’s previous observer. If no successor exists, the tail becomes the previous node instead. Removing the final node must leave both head and tail empty. These cases deserve explicit tests because a correct forward traversal can hide a stale backward link. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

keyPoints: A list prints one, three after removing two, so the first test passes.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 4, treat Failure clinic — Forward output hid a broken reverse chain as an algorithmic claim. The forward owner was repaired, but the successor’s previous observer still points to the removed node. The right repair is a structural update, not suppressing the reverse test. If appending after deleting the last element fails, inspect tail_. A stale observer may survive an otherwise empty head. Add the exact sequence “append, erase sole element, append again” as a regression. Testing only construction and destruction never crosses that reusable-empty-state boundary.
